rv.q: A tough, troubling, revealing play: proof again that the stage has become an excellent place to grapple, collectively, with our fraught and freighted times.

Harris's play is full of a sharp satirical intelligence that makes the right words fall from the wrong mouths, and resists pat conclusions.
...ebulliently messy, fiendishly clever, frequently maddening and gloriously different
It might be flawed but it is charismatic, needling theatre. An event.
The acting is both raw and precise, and O'Hara maintains a hair-trigger tension as Harris flings us between shock, hilarity and horror.
I have rarely seen a show that left me so cold – its provocations so evident, its expression frequently heavy – but so subsequently alive with questions.
It's never boring, but it's only the satirical side that works. The rest is a cluttered, taboo-busting ragbag of racial issues, with a big star thrown in.
Harris touches skillfully on the issue of illicit sexual fantasy... but he fails to convince us fully as to why at least two of these pairs might have thought such a high-risk gamble worth taking.
This controversial race drama doesn't work zeitgeist-defining magic
Jeremy O Harris's play comes across as the sort of ideas-led piece that would stimulate over an hour but has instead unwisely swollen to two hours.
But I couldn't help but feel that the play fails at what it sets out to do.
Suffice to say, it is a loveless piece of work, from which many people, of all ethnicities, may wish in retrospect that they too had been excluded.
Slave Play is unrelenting. It's a gripping and unapologetically challenging play with hard-to-stomach subject matter. But there's no doubt that it needs to be heard.
There is undoubtedly a pervading artificiality to the single-lens perspective through which the failures of the biracial relationships being examined are perceived.
The overall acting is a bit hammed, rich in strong, exaggerated movements and fighting scenes choreographed by Jade Hackett.
For a play that wears controversy as a badge of honour the last thing I expected to feel was slightly bored.
Writer Jeremy O. Harris is seeking to make the audience uncomfortable but to what end is never clear and, in the end, this play fails on nearly all accounts.
Slave Play is too obsessed with conceptual naval gazing to the extent that it forgets that its characters are human beings.
The play seems to reinforce the caricatures it sets out to diminish.
None of the sections is believable. The dialogue is artificial and makes the slight characterisation even less convincing.
It is enough to say bravely, wittily, with superb acting and not a little discomfort.
It's funny, clever and undoubtedly challenging, though neither as outrageous nor profound as it would like to be.
